text: What is the primary domain or field this prompt or project addresses? Describe its scope, core concerns, and any relevant sub-disciplines.

choices.text: A single well-established domain (e.g., machine learning, civil engineering)
An interdisciplinary space spanning 2-3 domains
An emerging or niche area with evolving terminology

answer:
SPACE (Superb Prompt Automatic Creation Engine) is a programmable specification engine that transforms structured elicitation probes into development specifications. It operates at the intersection of prompt engineering, software specification, and developer tooling.

The primary domain is software specification engineering augmented by LLM capabilities. Core concerns include: (1) Structured elicitation — systematically extracting domain knowledge from humans through a 326-probe questionnaire organized into 7 progressive series with 25 rounds. (2) Dependency-aware routing — ensuring questions are asked in an order that respects logical prerequisites, where later questions can reference artifacts from earlier ones. (3) Artifact extraction — automatically identifying and cataloging key design decisions, entity definitions, and architectural choices from free-text answers. (4) Multi-format export — generating specification documents in JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML, and LLM-consumable prompt formats.

Sub-disciplines encompassed: structured prompt engineering, dependency graph traversal, artifact mapping, specification generation, and progressive deepening methodologies. The system draws from elicitation techniques used in requirements engineering (specifically the JAD — Joint Application Development — facilitation model), ontological modeling from knowledge representation (OWL-style entity classification), and the progressive disclosure pattern from UX design. The domain also intersects with formal methods (the framework produces structured, machine-readable specifications) and knowledge management (the artifact dictionary becomes a living knowledge base for the project).

variants.architect: SPACE operates in the domain of software specification engineering augmented by LLM capabilities, sitting at the intersection of three well-established fields: requirements engineering, prompt engineering, and developer tooling. The architectural significance is that it treats specification creation as a structured data flow problem rather than a free-form documentation task. The dependency graph between the 7 series (Domain & Audience, Assumptions & Abstraction, etc.) follows a directed acyclic graph pattern where each series produces artifacts consumed by downstream series. This is architecturally analogous to a build system like Webpack where modules declare their dependencies. The core concern is converting unstructured human knowledge into structured, machine-readable specifications — a transformation problem that requires careful interface design between the elicitation layer (questions), the synthesis layer (artifact extraction), and the export layer (multi-format generation). The separation between FrameworkDefinition (the static 326-question schema) and SessionState (the runtime answer accumulator) follows the Command-Query Separation pattern, keeping the question structure immutable while session data mutates freely.
variants.practitioner: SPACE's domain maps directly to the src/ directory structure: src/engine/ handles the specification pipeline, src/storage/ persists session state, src/llm/ integrates providers for refinement and synthesis, src/export/ generates multi-format output, and web/ provides the browser interface. The 326 probes live in JSON framework definition files loaded by src/data/framework-loader.ts. When implementing new features, the practitioner needs to understand that Series 1 answers seed the artifact dictionary, which Series 2 reads to scope entity modeling, which Series 3 uses for relationship mapping — this is a pipeline where each stage's output becomes the next stage's input. The TypeScript types in src/types/index.ts define the contracts: FrameworkDefinition, SessionState, ArtifactDictionary. Any new feature must produce or consume artifacts that fit the ArtifactValue interface with its source_question_id, confidence, and derived_from fields. The 7 export formats in src/export/formatters/ each implement the same ExportResult interface, so adding a new format (like PDF) means implementing a single class that returns content, filename, mime_type, and size_bytes.
variants.strategist: The primary domain — structured specification generation for software projects — is underserved by existing tools. Current alternatives include Notion templates (manual, no automation), Google Docs (free-form, no structure), and AI chatbots (no systematic coverage). SPACE differentiates by offering deterministic, reproducible specification workflows backed by a validated 326-probe framework. The target market is mid-stage startups (Series A-C) and enterprise innovation teams who spend 2-4 weeks on requirements gathering before each sprint cycle. The value proposition is reducing this to 2-4 hours of structured input followed by automated spec generation. The competitive moat is the framework itself — the 326 probes encode domain expertise that would take teams months to develop independently. The go-to-market strategy should target developer communities (HN, dev.to, GitHub) with the CLI tool as a free OSS entry point, then upsell the web UI and team collaboration features. Success metric: reduce time-to-specification by 80% while maintaining or improving spec quality scores.
variants.critic: The domain classification is somewhat inflated. SPACE is fundamentally a structured questionnaire with artifact extraction and template-based export — calling it 'specification engineering' overstates the formal rigor. The 326 probes are pre-authored, not generated, so the 'automatic creation engine' moniker is misleading; it's more of a 'guided specification elicitation engine.' A skeptic would note that the LLM integration layer (src/llm/) adds significant complexity but unclear value — if the probes are well-designed, human answers should be sufficient without LLM refinement. The dependency graph between series, while elegant architecturally, creates a rigid workflow that may frustrate users who want to jump to specific sections. The sub-disciplines claimed (ontological modeling, JAD facilitation) are loosely borrowed; the system doesn't actually implement OWL-style reasoning or JAD's multi-stakeholder facilitation. The real risk is that the domain is too niche: developers who need specs usually just write them, and those who don't won't be motivated by a 326-question questionnaire regardless of how well-structured it is.

text: Who is the intended audience for the generated output? What is their baseline familiarity with this domain?

choices.text: Experts / researchers — people who work in this domain daily
Practitioners / professionals — experienced but may need refreshers
Learners / general audience — minimal assumed knowledge

answer:
The primary audience is software developers and technical leads building LLM-powered applications or complex systems who need structured specifications. These are practitioners who understand TypeScript/Node.js, have experience with CLI tools and web frameworks, and are comfortable with JSON/YAML data structures.

Secondary audiences: (1) Product managers who need to formalize requirements for AI-assisted development — they provide domain context but expect the framework to structure it. (2) Architects designing systems that integrate multiple LLM providers — they need the framework to capture cross-cutting concerns like provider fallback, cost budgets, and latency targets. (3) Open-source maintainers who want to document their projects systematically — the framework produces a comprehensive specification that doubles as project documentation. (4) Technical writers who need structured input for generating documentation — the exported specifications feed directly into documentation pipelines.

Baseline familiarity: respondents understand REST APIs, npm ecosystems, and basic AI/ML concepts. They have likely used at least one LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Mistral, or Ollama) and understand the difference between system prompts, user prompts, and completion endpoints. They may not be familiar with ontological modeling or dependency graph theory, so the framework explains these concepts progressively through Series 1. The audience profile directly informs the verbosity level (moderate), abstraction level (mixed concrete/formal), and terminology choices (industry standard with definitions for novel terms) across the entire framework.

variants.architect: The audience segmentation reveals distinct interface requirements that should influence the system's layering. Practitioners (TypeScript developers) interact with the CLI in src/cli/ and need programmatic access to artifacts. Product managers interact via the web UI in web/ and need visual progress tracking and export capabilities. Architects need the full artifact dictionary and dependency graph visualization. The baseline familiarity assumption — that users understand REST APIs, npm, and LLM concepts — directly constrains the error handling strategy in src/engine/validator.ts: validation errors should reference question IDs and artifact keys, not internal state representations. The audience profile also shapes the context_template field in OpenEndedQuestion: templates should assume knowledge of basic software engineering but explain SPACE-specific concepts like 'artifact dictionary' and 'series dependency' inline. The secondary audiences (maintainers, technical writers) consume exported artifacts, not the elicitation engine itself, which justifies the clean separation between src/engine/ (internal) and src/export/ (external consumption).
variants.practitioner: The audience split determines implementation priorities. For CLI practitioners, the key files are src/cli/commands/run.ts (interactive questioning) and src/cli/commands/export.ts (output generation). The run command needs to handle the full session lifecycle: init → question display → answer collection → artifact extraction → progress tracking → next question routing. For the web audience, web/server.mjs serves the React frontend that needs to implement the same flow through a browser interface. The baseline familiarity with npm means we can use chalk, inquirer, and other CLI libraries without extensive onboarding docs. The TypeScript audience expects strong typing, so all public APIs in src/types/index.ts should be well-documented with JSDoc. The storage layer (src/storage/sqlite.ts and src/storage/filesystem.ts) should support both backends since practitioners may prefer SQLite for performance while maintainers may prefer filesystem for portability. Testing the audience assumption means verifying that the context_template on each question in the framework JSON files is sufficient for someone unfamiliar with SPACE terminology.
variants.strategist: The practitioner-first audience strategy is correct for developer tool adoption — OSS CLI tools win when they're immediately useful without onboarding friction. However, the product manager secondary audience is underserved by the current architecture. PMs won't use a CLI; they need the web UI (web/) to be production-ready before any PM-facing marketing. The technical writer audience is the fastest path to viral adoption: if SPACE specs become the input format for documentation generators (Docusaurus, GitBook, ReadMe), each technical writer who adopts SPACE creates a multiplier effect. The roadmap should prioritize: (1) CLI for developers (MVP, months 1-3), (2) Web UI for PMs (months 4-6), (3) Export integration with doc platforms (months 7-9). The open-source maintainer audience is attractive but small; they're better served as evangelists than primary users. Key success metric: time from npm install to first completed session should be under 10 minutes for a developer who has read the README.
variants.critic: The audience definition is too broad and internally contradictory. A 'TypeScript developer building LLM-powered applications' is a very specific persona — these are early adopters building with OpenAI/Anthropic APIs, not the mainstream developer population. Assuming they understand 'npm ecosystems and basic AI/ML concepts' may alienate the larger market of developers who build traditional CRUD apps and could benefit from structured specs. The claim that 'technical writers need structured input for generating documentation pipelines' is aspirational; most technical writers use Markdown in Git repos and would not adopt a 326-question tool for documentation. The framework's explanatory approach ('explains these concepts progressively through Series 1') assumes users will complete all 326 questions, but completion rates for long structured inputs are typically below 15%. The real audience is likely much narrower: technically sophisticated developers who are already bought into structured specification methodologies (like Behavior-Driven Development practitioners) and are looking for a more comprehensive framework. Marketing to a broader audience risks disappointing users who expect a simpler tool.

text: What foundational concepts, theorems, or prior art can the output take for granted? What must be explained from scratch?

choices.text: Full prerequisites assumed — dive straight into advanced material
Core fundamentals assumed; edge cases and advanced topics explained
First-principles treatment — no prior knowledge assumed

answer:
Assumed knowledge that the output can take for granted: CLI tool usage (npm install, git clone, running scripts), Node.js/TypeScript basics (import/export, async/await, type annotations, interfaces), JSON/YAML parsing and structure, REST API concepts (endpoints, request/response, status codes), prompt engineering fundamentals (system prompts, few-shot prompting, temperature, top_p), and basic software architecture patterns (MVC, event-driven, plugin systems, dependency injection).

Must be explained from scratch: (1) The specific 7-series progressive elicitation methodology — how questions build on each other across series in a dependency graph. (2) The dependency chain between series — why Series 2 (Ontological Characteristics) cannot start until Series 1 (Conceptual Depth) provides domain and audience context, and why Series 7 (Operational/Functional) depends on both Series 5 and 6. (3) How artifacts accumulate — each answer contributes extracted data (entity lists, relationship graphs, procedure steps, tech stack decisions) that downstream series consume via the artifact dictionary. (4) The 326-probe structure — 67 open-ended questions, each with 3-5 multi-choice follow-ups that classify and clarify the answer, totaling 201+ follow-up choices. (5) How the framework produces a coherent specification from apparently disconnected questions through the artifact dependency graph. (6) The StorageProvider abstraction — how sessions persist via filesystem or SQLite. (7) The LLM provider factory — how multiple AI backends (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama) are abstracted behind a unified interface.

variants.architect: SPACE can take for granted foundational software engineering concepts: module systems, async control flow, type systems, and data serialization. The output can assume familiarity with the TypeScript ecosystem (interfaces, generics, union types) since the entire codebase is TypeScript. However, several concepts must be introduced from scratch: the FrameworkDefinition structure (the 7-series hierarchy is SPACE-specific), the ArtifactDictionary pattern (a dynamic key-value store where keys are semantically meaningful and values carry provenance metadata), and the dependency graph model (how series consume artifacts from predecessor series). The JAD facilitation model should be referenced but not assumed — the system's progressive questioning approach borrows from JAD but operates differently. The OWL-style ontological modeling reference is aspirational; the system extracts entity definitions from free-text answers but does not implement formal reasoning. What must be explained from scratch: the concept of a 'probe' (a structured question designed to elicit specific information), the 'artifact' as a living document that evolves across series, and the snapshot mechanism for preserving intermediate state.
variants.practitioner: The prior art SPACE can leverage includes: dependency graph implementations (topological sort in src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts), state machine patterns for session lifecycle (created → in_progress → completed), and repository pattern for storage (src/storage/types.ts defines the StorageProvider interface). The practitioner should reference existing TypeScript patterns: discriminated unions for SpaceEvent types (already in types/index.ts), branded types for session/project IDs, and the builder pattern for ExportOptions. Concepts requiring explanation from scratch: the context_template interpolation system (how question text adapts based on prior artifacts), the artifact confidence scoring (0.0-1.0 scale in ArtifactValue), and the quality scoring dimensions in src/llm/quality-scorer.ts (completeness, specificity, consistency, actionability). The completeness-scorer in src/intelligence/ implements a custom scoring algorithm that doesn't follow standard heuristics — this needs API docs. The snapshot-manager.ts creates periodic checkpoints during sessions, which is an uncommon pattern in CLI tools that practitioners may not expect.
variants.strategist: Prior art the market recognizes: ChatGPT for ad-hoc prompting, Jasper/Copy.ai for content generation templates, and Notion AI for document augmentation. SPACE differentiates by being specification-focused rather than content-focused. The concepts it must explain from scratch (probe-based elicitation, artifact dictionaries, series dependencies) are its unique value props and competitive moat — these are the innovations that justify a standalone tool rather than a ChatGPT plugin. The risk is that explaining these concepts requires significant documentation investment. The strategy should be: invest heavily in the first-session experience (guided walkthrough with pre-filled example answers) so users learn by doing rather than reading. The 'prior art' positioning matters for investor conversations: frame SPACE as 'requirements engineering meets prompt engineering' rather than 'a complex questionnaire tool.' The emerging area recognition is important — the tooling market for AI-assisted development is pre-Category, meaning the first well-positioned tool can define the category.
variants.critic: The assumption that users understand 'CLI tool usage, npm, and TypeScript basics' is already a significant filter that excludes most software professionals. The real issue is that the 'foundational concepts' SPACE requires aren't just technical — they include an entire methodology (structured elicitation, progressive deepening, artifact dictionaries) that has no mainstream precedent. This means SPACE is simultaneously trying to introduce a new methodology AND build tooling for it, which is a much harder go-to-market challenge than building tooling for an established methodology. The JAD reference is problematic: Joint Application Development was popular in the 1990s enterprise space and is largely forgotten. Referencing it adds no value for the target audience. The OWL-style ontology claim should be dropped entirely — the system does simple key-value artifact extraction, not formal ontological reasoning. Being honest about what the system does (structured questioning with artifact extraction and multi-format export) is more compelling than dressing it up with academic terminology. The assumption that 'the artifact dictionary becomes a living knowledge base' is only true if users return to the tool repeatedly, which assumes a retention mechanism that doesn't exist in the current design.

text: At what level of abstraction should the output operate? Should it be concrete and example-driven, or formal and general?

choices.text: Concrete — specific examples, code snippets, case studies
Mixed — conceptual frameworks illustrated with examples
Formal — definitions, proofs, mathematical notation, first-order logic

answer:
Mixed approach — present the SPACE architecture with clear structural diagrams showing the series dependency graph and question flow, then ground each concept with concrete examples from the actual codebase.

For the structural layer: use dependency graphs (Series 1 feeds Series 2, which feeds Series 3; Series 2+3 feed Series 4; Series 1+4 feed Series 5; Series 4+5 feed Series 6; Series 5+6 feed Series 7) to show the progressive narrowing. Show how each series consumes artifacts from previous series via the artifact dictionary. Show the series/round/question hierarchy with the z_multi_choice_per_open parameter controlling follow-up depth.

For the concrete layer: show actual TypeScript code snippets from the engine (question-router.ts showing dependency resolution, session-manager.ts showing state transitions, artifact-mapping.ts showing extraction patterns), real JSON examples of session state (with question answers, artifact dictionaries, and completion flags), and actual output from the export pipeline (JSON spec, Markdown doc, YAML config, HTML report, LLM prompt). The abstraction level balances formal definitions (the StorageProvider interface, the LLMProvider interface, the SpaceConfig type) with illustrative examples (actual terminal output from "space run", actual JSON artifact entries).

variants.architect: The mixed abstraction approach is architecturally sound because SPACE operates at multiple levels simultaneously: the question framework (abstract, declarative), the engine (concrete, imperative), and the LLM integration (probabilistic, contextual). Presenting the dependency graph as a structural diagram first grounds the reader in the system's topology, then concrete code examples from src/engine/question-router.ts demonstrate how the abstract graph is traversed at runtime. The key architectural insight is that the system has two distinct abstraction layers: (1) the framework definition layer (JSON files, immutable, purely declarative) and (2) the session/execution layer (TypeScript runtime, mutable state, imperative logic). The abstraction level should shift as the document progresses: Series 1 answers establish conceptual grounding (abstract), Series 2-3 build the entity model (semi-formal), and Series 4-7 specify implementation details (concrete). This mirrors the actual codebase structure where src/types/ is abstract, src/engine/ is semi-abstract, and src/cli/ is concrete.
variants.practitioner: The concrete examples should ground each concept in actual code paths. For example, when explaining the dependency graph, show how src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts implements topological sort over the DependencyGraph type from src/types/index.ts. When explaining artifact extraction, show how src/data/artifact-mapping.ts transforms free-text AnswerEntry values into structured ArtifactValue objects. The session lifecycle can be demonstrated by walking through src/engine/session-manager.ts: session.create() → session.submitAnswer() → session.nextQuestion() → session.export(). Each code example should include the function signature, a brief usage pattern, and the relevant type contract. The engine's core loop (in src/engine/core.ts) is the most concrete demonstration: it shows how the system moves from question to question, checks dependencies, extracts artifacts, and tracks progress. Concrete error handling examples should reference src/engine/validator.ts patterns like ValidationResult and the error code conventions used in SpaceEvent.
variants.strategist: The abstraction level decision directly impacts developer adoption speed. If SPACE starts too abstract (methodology-first), developers will lose interest before seeing working code. If it starts too concrete (install-and-run), they won't understand the 326-probe framework's value. The recommended approach for the web audience: lead with the output (a sample specification generated by SPACE) then work backward to the methodology. For the CLI audience: lead with the command (npx space init) and let the progressive questioning demonstrate the methodology in practice. The strategic document should maintain two parallel tracks: a 'quick start' (concrete, 5 minutes to first spec) and a 'deep dive' (abstract, comprehensive architecture explanation). Market data suggests developer tools with both tracks see 3x higher conversion than tools that only offer one. The output abstraction level should match the audience's decision-making needs: PMs need the output (what does a SPACE spec look like?), architects need the architecture (how does the system work?), and developers need the code (how do I implement this?).
variants.critic: The mixed abstraction approach risks incoherence. If the document starts abstract and shifts to concrete without clear signposting, readers will be disoriented. The claim that it 'grounds each concept with concrete examples from the actual codebase' assumes the codebase is stable enough to reference — in an active development phase, code examples rot quickly. A more robust approach would be to keep the specification abstract and provide a separate 'implementation guide' with code examples that can be updated independently. The progressive deepening described ('Series 1 establishes grounding, Series 2-3 builds entities, Series 4-7 specifies details') sounds elegant but may not survive contact with real users who want to skip ahead. The abstraction level assumption also fails for the web audience: web users expect instant visual feedback, not progressive methodology revelation. The biggest flaw is assuming that one document format can serve both the architect (who wants diagrams) and the practitioner (who wants code). These are different documents for different audiences, and trying to serve both dilutes both.

text: What vocabulary, jargon, or notation should be used or deliberately avoided? Are there established standards the output should follow?

choices.text: Standard industry terminology — use common terms precisely
Plain accessible language — minimize jargon; explain what is used
Formal academic register — precise definitions, technical notation

answer:
Standard software engineering terminology used consistently throughout: session (a user interaction instance with a unique UUID), artifact (extracted structured data from answers, stored in the artifact dictionary), framework (the 326-probe question set defined in JSON), series (a themed group of rounds, 7 total), round (a batch of 2-5 related open-ended questions), probe (a single elicitation question — open-ended or multi-choice follow-up), dependency (a series that must complete before another can start).

Industry terms used precisely: dependency injection (for the StorageProvider pattern allowing filesystem or SQLite backends), factory pattern (for LLM provider creation via createLLMProvider()), event emitter (for lifecycle hooks in the session manager), command pattern (for CLI commands in src/cli/commands/), strategy pattern (for export format selection), adapter pattern (for the StorageProvider implementations).

Terms deliberately avoided: "AI" or "intelligent" for the engine (it routes and extracts deterministically, not "understands"), "user" for the respondent (use "respondent" or "answerer" to distinguish from system operators), "generate" for the export (use "compile" or "render" to distinguish from LLM generation), "smart" for any feature (avoid marketing language in technical specifications), "revolutionary" or "groundbreaking" for the methodology (it's a practical engineering tool, not a research paper).

Notation conventions: question IDs use dot notation (e.g., "2.3.1" = Series 2, Round 3, Question 1). Artifact keys use snake_case (e.g., "entity_list", "relationship_graph"). File paths use forward slashes. Code references use backtick formatting.

variants.architect: SPACE establishes a domain-specific vocabulary that must be used with absolute consistency across all interfaces — CLI output, web UI, exported specs, and documentation. Key terms that carry architectural significance: 'session' (a bounded execution context, not a user session), 'artifact' (derived structured data, not a build artifact), 'series' (a question group, not a data series), 'round' (a progressive step within a series), 'probe' (an elicitation question, not a network probe). The vocabulary follows the Adapter pattern — mapping general concepts to SPACE-specific terms. The notation conventions should follow JSON Schema patterns for the framework definition files and TypeScript conventions for the codebase. Terms to deliberately avoid: 'prompt' (confusing with LLM prompts — SPACE uses 'question' or 'probe'), 'model' (confusing with ML models — SPACE uses 'framework' or 'entity'), 'template' (confusing with HTML templates — SPACE uses 'context_template' for the specific field). The established standard is: all SPACE-specific terms are lowercase with underscores (snake_case), matching the JSON framework file convention.
variants.practitioner: In the codebase, terminology is enforced through TypeScript types in src/types/index.ts. The interface names serve as vocabulary anchors: SessionState, ArtifactDictionary, FrameworkDefinition, QuestionContext. When implementing new features, developers must use these exact type names — not synonyms. The src/cli/tui.ts and web/ should display the same terminology to users. For example, the CLI shows 'Series 2: Ontological Characteristics' and the web UI must show the identical label. The artifact key naming convention (e.g., 'entity_list', 'domain_scope', 'tech_stack') should be documented in src/data/artifact-mapping.ts with JSDoc comments explaining each key's semantic meaning. When writing tests, test descriptions should use the canonical terminology: 'should complete round when all questions answered' not 'should finish step when all prompts done.' The context_template interpolation system uses {{artifact_key}} placeholders that reference the artifact dictionary — the syntax is Mustache-style (double curly braces) and should not be confused with TypeScript template literals.
variants.strategist: The terminology choice directly impacts SEO, community building, and market positioning. 'Probe' is more distinctive than 'question' and creates a unique search identity — when users search 'SPACE probes' or 'elicitation probes,' the tool owns that keyword space. 'Artifact' is problematic because it collides with Maven/Gradle build artifacts in developer search results. Consider 'spec artifact' or 'design artifact' as a compound term to differentiate. The vocabulary decisions should be finalized before any public documentation is published — changing terminology after launch creates migration pain and community confusion. The established standards alignment matters for integration: if SPACE artifacts follow JSON Schema conventions, they can be consumed by tools like Postman, Swagger, and OpenAPI generators, which expands the addressable market. The deliberate avoidance of 'prompt' is strategically important — it positions SPACE as distinct from prompt engineering tools, which is correct because SPACE is a specification tool that happens to use LLMs, not a prompt engineering tool that happens to generate specs.
variants.critic: The terminology enforcement is inconsistent across the existing codebase. The CLI in src/cli/tui.ts uses 'Question' in user-facing text, while the artifact system refers to 'probes.' The web UI (web/) likely has its own terminology choices. This inconsistency will confuse users who see different terms for the same concept across interfaces. The snake_case convention for artifact keys ('entity_list', 'domain_scope') is developer-friendly but not user-friendly — the web UI should present these as human-readable labels ('Entity List', 'Domain Scope') while maintaining the snake_case keys internally. The biggest vocabulary problem is 'session' — in web development, 'session' universally means 'user authentication state,' so using it for 'a run through the questionnaire' will cause confusion. A better term would be 'survey run' or 'spec run.' The deliberate avoidance of 'template' is undermined by the framework itself using context_template as a field name. The claim that terminology follows 'JSON Schema patterns' is aspirational — the framework JSON files use a custom format that doesn't conform to JSON Schema's vocabulary.

text: How should complexity be distributed across the output? Should it start simple and deepen, or maintain a consistent level throughout?

choices.text: Progressive — scaffold from simple foundations to advanced topics
Flat — consistent complexity level throughout
Overview-first — high-level summary then independent deep dives

answer:
Progressive scaffolding — start with the simple concept of asking structured questions to produce specifications, then layer in complexity one dimension at a time:

Layer 1 (Series 1): Question asking — the basic loop of presenting questions and recording answers. Establish domain, audience, vocabulary, and abstraction level. This is the simplest concept and requires no prerequisite knowledge.

Layer 2 (Series 2): Entity discovery — identify the primary entities, attributes, categories, and boundaries of the domain. Introduce the concept of ontological modeling (but call it "entity mapping" for accessibility). Show how free-text answers are parsed for entity mentions.

Layer 3 (Series 3): Relationship mapping — connect entities with associations, hierarchies, causal chains, and dependencies. Introduce graph theory concepts (nodes, edges, directed graphs) through concrete examples.

Layer 4 (Series 4): Procedural scoping — define workflows, decision points, error handling, and step granularity. Connect procedures to entities (procedures operate on entities) and relationships (procedures traverse relationships).

Layer 5 (Series 5): Technical specifications — hardware, software, performance, security, integrations, and timeline. This is the most concrete layer and grounds all previous abstract concepts in specific technology choices.

Layer 6 (Series 6): Development methodology — team process, quality practices, communication patterns. Connects technical specifications to human organization.

Layer 7 (Series 7): Operational preferences — deployment, monitoring, maintenance, stewardship. The final layer that ensures the specification is actionable.

Each layer builds on all previous layers. The complexity distribution is deliberately front-loaded: Series 1-2 introduce the most new concepts, Series 3-4 apply them, Series 5-7 ground them in specifics. This matches the progressive disclosure pattern where users learn the framework by doing, not by reading documentation.

variants.architect: The progressive complexity distribution follows the Layered Architecture pattern, where each layer builds on the previous one's abstractions. Layer 1 (Series 1) establishes the vocabulary and basic data model — FrameworkDefinition, SessionState. Layer 2 (Series 2-3) introduces the artifact extraction pipeline and dependency resolution. Layer 3 (Series 4-5) adds LLM integration and quality scoring. Layer 4 (Series 6-7) specifies export formats and deployment. This layering maps directly to the src/ directory structure: types/ → engine/ → llm/ → export/. The architectural benefit is that each layer can be understood, tested, and modified independently. The risk of this approach is that users who only complete Series 1-2 will have an incomplete mental model of the system's full capabilities. The mitigation is that each series' output (exported specification) should be independently useful, not just a stepping stone to the full specification.
variants.practitioner: The progressive scaffolding should mirror the actual implementation order. In src/engine/core.ts, the core loop starts with the simplest case: load framework → display question → collect answer → extract artifacts → route to next question. Each subsequent file adds complexity: dependency-resolver.ts adds graph traversal, validator.ts adds answer quality checks, snapshot-manager.ts adds state persistence, session-manager.ts adds resume/abandon lifecycle. The implementation should follow this same progressive pattern in tests: first test the basic question-answer loop, then add dependency resolution, then add artifact extraction, then add LLM refinement. The complexity distribution in user-facing output (CLI and web) should match: the initial questions are simple and self-contained, later questions reference earlier artifacts ('Based on your earlier answer about [entity_list], which relationships exist between...'). The context_template field on each OpenEndedQuestion drives this progressive revelation — earlier questions have no context_template, later ones interpolate prior artifacts.
variants.strategist: Progressive scaffolding is the right approach for developer tool adoption — it's the pattern used by successful tools like Vite (zero-config start, optional customization), Next.js (file-based routing, optional API routes), and Prisma (simple schema, optional migrations). The strategic benefit is a low barrier to entry (first question takes 30 seconds) with increasing depth (full specification takes 2-4 hours). The risk is that the 'progressive' part becomes 'prolonged' — if Series 1-2 feel like busywork before the interesting stuff arrives, users will abandon. The mitigation is to ensure each series produces immediately useful output: after Series 2, the user should have a usable entity list. After Series 4, they should have a working prototype prompt. The product strategy should market the 'minimum viable specification' (after Series 2-3, approximately 60 questions) as a complete product for simple projects, with Series 4-7 as optional depth for complex projects. This creates a natural upsell path from the free CLI (basic questions) to the web UI (full 326-probe experience with visualization).
variants.critic: The progressive scaffolding assumption breaks down in practice because SPACE's 326 questions are front-loaded with methodology questions (Series 1: Domain & Audience, Assumptions & Abstraction) that most practitioners will find tedious. The 'simple to deep' progression assumes users are learning the methodology as they answer, but most developers just want to describe their project and get a spec — they don't want to first articulate their 'primary domain,' 'intended audience,' and 'foundational concepts.' A better approach would be to invert the progression: start with the concrete (what are you building? what entities does it have? how do they relate?) and derive the abstract (what domain is this? who is the audience?) as downstream inferences. The claim that 'each series' output should be independently useful' is aspirational — a specification that only covers domain/audience and entity discovery (Series 1-2) is not useful as a development spec. The complexity distribution also fails for the web UI: web users expect visual feedback (charts, progress bars, entity diagrams) which adds implementation complexity that the CLI doesn't face. The progressive model is a content architecture decision being presented as a UX decision, and these serve different masters.

text: What are the primary entities, objects, concepts, or actors that exist in this domain? List them with brief descriptions.

choices.text: Fewer than 5 core entities — the domain is compact and well-bounded
5–10 entities — moderate complexity with clear boundaries
10–20 entities — rich domain with distinct sub-areas
20+ entities — large domain requiring hierarchical organization
Uncertain — exploration may reveal entities not yet known

answer:
Core entities identified through systematic domain analysis of the SPACE system:

1. Framework — The 326-probe question set. Contains 7 series, each with multiple rounds, each round with 2-5 open-ended questions, each question with 3-5 multi-choice follow-ups. Defined in JSON files under prompt-framework/json/. Immutable after creation; the framework is the reference specification.

2. Series — A themed group of rounds within the framework. 7 series total: Conceptual Depth, Ontological Characteristics, Semantic Relationships, Procedural Breadth, Technical Specifications, Development Methodologies, Operational/Functional. Each series has dependencies (other series that must complete first), consumes (artifacts it needs), and provides (artifacts it produces).

3. Round — A batch of related open-ended questions within a series. Each round has a focus area (e.g., "Entity Discovery", "System Boundaries") and contains 2-5 questions that share thematic coherence.

4. Question — A single elicitation probe. Two types: open-ended (free text response) and multi-choice follow-up (classify the open-ended answer). Each question has a unique ID (e.g., "2.3.1"), text (the question prompt), and follow_up_choices (2-5 options).

5. Answer — A respondent's response to a question. Contains the open-ended text (the free response) and the chosen follow-up option (the classification). Answers are stored in session state.

6. Artifact — Structured data extracted from answers. Created by the artifact mapping system which parses free-text answers for entity mentions, architectural decisions, technology choices, and constraints. Artifacts accumulate across series and are consumed by downstream series.

7. Session — A complete interaction instance. Has a UUID, project association, current question pointer, answer history, artifact dictionary, and completion status. Sessions can be resumed from storage.

8. Project — A named workspace. Contains sessions, exports, and configuration. Stored in ~/.space/projects/<name>/.

9. Export — A compiled specification document. Multiple formats: JSON, Markdown, YAML, HTML, LLM prompt. Generated on-demand from session state and artifact dictionary.

10. Engine — The orchestration layer. Manages question routing, answer validation, artifact extraction, and session lifecycle. The core runtime that ties everything together.

variants.architect: The primary entity model follows the Aggregate pattern from Domain-Driven Design. The Framework aggregate root contains Series, which contain Rounds, which contain Questions, which contain Choices — this is a strict containment hierarchy where child entities cannot exist without their parent. Session is the runtime aggregate root that accumulates Answers and the ArtifactDictionary. The dependency graph (DependencyGraph with DependencyNode and DependencyEdge) exists outside both aggregates, connecting Series definitions to their artifact dependencies. The Project aggregate wraps multiple Sessions, supporting the use case of iterating on a specification across sessions. Architecturally, the clean separation between FrameworkDefinition (read-only schema) and SessionState (mutable runtime) follows CQRS principles — the query side reads the framework, the command side writes answers and extracts artifacts. The entities should be modeled as immutable value objects within the Framework aggregate and as mutable entities within the Session aggregate.
variants.practitioner: The entity list maps to TypeScript interfaces in src/types/index.ts. FrameworkDefinition → Framework, SeriesDefinition → Series, RoundDefinition → Round, OpenEndedQuestion → Question, MultiChoice → Choice. These are the 'definition' types (static, loaded from JSON). SessionMeta, AnswerEntry, ArtifactValue, ProgressState are the 'runtime' types (mutable, persisted to storage). The src/data/framework-loader.ts reads JSON files and produces FrameworkDefinition objects. The src/engine/question-router.ts traverses the framework's series/round/question hierarchy using the SeriesDefinition.rounds array. The src/data/artifact-mapping.ts defines the mapping between question IDs and artifact keys — this is the critical bridge between the definition layer and the runtime layer. When implementing new entity types, check if they belong in the definition layer (add to FrameworkDefinition side) or the runtime layer (add to SessionState side). The storage layer (src/storage/types.ts) defines how entities are serialized to SQLite or filesystem.
variants.strategist: The entity model is the foundation for all product features. The Framework entity (the 326-question structure) is the primary intellectual property — it encodes the methodology that differentiates SPACE. The Session entity represents the user's work product — completed sessions are the output users value and share. The ArtifactDictionary is the bridge between input (answers) and output (specifications) — it's where AI augmentation adds the most value through extraction and refinement. The Project entity supports team use cases (multiple sessions for the same project, compare-and-merge workflows) that justify paid tiers. Product roadmap should prioritize: (1) Framework authoring tools (let users customize the 326 probes), (2) Session sharing (let team members see each other's answers), (3) Artifact visualization (entity relationship diagrams from the artifact dictionary). The entity model's clean separation between definition and runtime enables a marketplace where users can author and share custom frameworks — a significant revenue opportunity.
variants.critic: The entity list has gaps. There's no 'User' or 'Respondent' entity — the system assumes a single user per session, but real-world use cases involve multiple stakeholders answering different questions. The 'Choice' entity (MultiChoice) conflates two different things: pre-authored follow-up choices (part of the framework definition) and user selections (part of the answer). The src/types/index.ts uses 'MultiChoice' for the definition side and 'multi_choice_id' in AnswerEntry for the selection, which is correct but the naming creates confusion. More critically, there's no 'Version' entity — when the framework is updated (new probes added, existing ones modified), there's no mechanism to track which version of the framework a session was created against, despite framework_version appearing as a string field. The entity model also lacks a 'Tag' or 'Label' entity for categorizing artifacts, which will be needed for the export layer to group related artifacts. The DependencyGraph being separate from the Framework entity is an architectural smell — it should be embedded within the Framework definition.

text: What attributes, properties, or state define each entity? How do entities differ from one another?

choices.text: 1–2 key attributes per entity — simple identifiers suffice
3–5 attributes per entity — moderate descriptive richness
6–10 attributes per entity — detailed characterization
10+ attributes per entity — comprehensive with optional fields
Highly variable — attributes differ significantly across entities

answer:
Entity attributes with types and constraints:

Framework: id (number, 1-7 range), name (string, 3-50 chars), description (string, 50-200 chars), x_rounds (number), y_open_ended_per_round (number), z_multi_choice_per_open (number), depends_on (number[]), provides (string[]), consumes (string[]).

Series: id (number, 1-7), name (string), description (string), rounds (Round[]), deps (number[]). Attributes differ from Framework because Series is the runtime representation while Framework is the definition format.

Round: round (number, 1-based within series), focus (string, 2-20 words), questions (Question[]).

Question: id (string, dot notation e.g., "2.3.1"), text (string, 10-200 chars), follow_up_choices (Choice[]), type ("open_ended" | "multi_choice_follow_up").

Answer: question_id (string, FK to Question), open_ended (string, 10-5000 chars), choice_id (string, FK to Choice), timestamp (ISO 8601).

Artifact: key (string, snake_case), value (any — string, number, array, object), source_question_id (string, FK), series_origin (number), confidence (number, 0-1).

Session: id (UUID string), project_id (string, FK), current_question_id (string | null), answers (Answer[]), artifacts (Record<string, any>), status ("active" | "completed" | "paused"), created_at (ISO 8601), updated_at (ISO 8601).

Project: name (string, kebab-case), description (string), created_at (ISO 8601), sessions (Session[]), exports (Export[]).

Export: session_id (string, FK), format ("json" | "markdown" | "yaml" | "html" | "llm_prompt"), content (string), filename (string), generated_at (ISO 8601).

Engine: config (SpaceConfig), storage (StorageProvider), llm (LLMProvider | null), state (SessionState).

variants.architect: Entity attributes follow the DDD value object pattern where identity is defined by the combination of key attributes rather than a surrogate ID. For FrameworkDefinition entities, the id field (series number, round number, question ID string) serves as a natural key derived from the hierarchy path. For SessionState entities, the id is a UUID assigned at creation time. The differentiation between entity types is driven by their attribute sets: SeriesDefinition has depends_on/consumes/provides (relationship metadata), RoundDefinition has focus (thematic grouping), OpenEndedQuestion has context_template (dynamic content), and MultiChoice has weight (selection influence). The attribute types follow a consistent convention: strings for display values, numbers for ordering/scoring, booleans for flags, arrays for collections, and Record types for key-value mappings. The ArtifactValue interface is notable for including confidence (0.0-1.0) and source_question_id — these provenance attributes enable the intelligence layer in src/intelligence/ to assess quality and traceability.
variants.practitioner: Each entity's attributes map to specific implementation concerns. SessionMeta.status uses a TypeScript string literal union ('created' | 'in_progress' | 'completed' | 'abandoned') — this is a state machine pattern where transitions are managed by session-manager.ts. AnswerEntry includes edit_count and quality_score for the intelligence layer — these are updated by src/llm/quality-scorer.ts after each answer submission. ArtifactValue.value is typed as 'any', which is a deliberate flexibility trade-off — artifact values can be strings, arrays, objects, or primitives depending on the extraction logic in src/data/artifact-mapping.ts. The ProgressState entity tracks completed_rounds and completed_series as arrays of strings/numbers — these are denormalized for O(1) lookup during progress calculations in src/engine/progress.ts. The LLMMetadata entity tracks token usage per session, enabling cost monitoring — the total_tokens_used field is incremented by each LLM provider in src/llm/providers/.
variants.strategist: The attribute design reveals product priorities. The quality_score on AnswerEntry suggests that answer quality matters — this enables a 'quality gate' feature where users cannot proceed to the next series until answers meet a threshold, which differentiates SPACE from simple questionnaire tools. The confidence field on ArtifactValue enables a 'low confidence' alert system that prompts users to refine vague answers. These intelligence features justify the premium pricing tier. The edit_count attribute suggests SPACE tracks iteration — this can power a 'revision history' feature that shows how specifications evolve. The framework_version field on SessionMeta enables backward compatibility — when SPACE releases a new framework version, users can still access sessions created with older versions. The lack of a 'priority' or 'importance' attribute on AnswerEntry is a product gap — not all 326 questions are equally important for every project, and a priority system would let users focus on the most impactful questions first.
variants.critic: The ArtifactValue.value typed as 'any' is a significant type safety violation. While it provides flexibility, it means the artifact dictionary cannot be validated at compile time — a typo in a key like 'entity_lsit' instead of 'entity_list' won't be caught until runtime. A better approach would be a typed artifact registry where each known artifact key has a defined value type. The quality_score on AnswerEntry (0.0-1.0) is dangerously vague — what does a 0.7 quality score mean? Without dimension-specific scoring (the QualityResult interface in types/index.ts has completeness/specificity/consistency/actionability but this isn't used on AnswerEntry), the single score is meaningless. The edit_count attribute suggests a 'mutable answers' model, but the dependency graph assumes answers are stable once submitted — if a user edits a Series 1 answer after completing Series 3, downstream artifacts may become inconsistent. The framework_version field is a string with no schema — there's no mechanism to compare versions or detect incompatibilities. The ProgressState.completed_rounds being stored as string[] means progress tracking requires array scanning rather than a more efficient set or bitmap.

text: What natural categories, types, or groupings organize these entities? Are there clear taxonomies or classification schemes?

choices.text: A single flat list — no meaningful sub-groupings
2–3 broad categories partitioning the entities
A shallow hierarchy (2 levels deep) of types and subtypes
A deep hierarchy (3+ levels) with inheritance
Multiple overlapping classification axes (e.g., by function and by scale)

answer:
Three natural categories emerge from functional analysis:

Category 1 — Structural Entities (define the system's shape): Framework, Series, Round, Question. These are the static definition entities that don't change during a session. They define WHAT gets asked and in what order. The dependency graph lives here — Series dependencies create a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that determines execution order.

Category 2 — Runtime Entities (capture the session's state): Session, Answer, Artifact. These are the dynamic entities that change as the session progresses. They capture WHAT was answered and what was extracted. The artifact dictionary is the central data structure here — it accumulates across all series.

Category 3 — Output Entities (produce the deliverables): Project, Export, Engine. These are the container and delivery entities. Projects hold sessions, Exports hold compiled specifications, and the Engine orchestrates everything.

The categories map to architectural layers: structural → data model (JSON schema definitions), runtime → engine layer (session management, artifact extraction), output → export layer (format compilation, file I/O). The dependency graph creates cross-category relationships where structural entities (Series) consume output entities (Artifacts) from other structural entities — this is the key insight that makes the framework self-referential.

The category boundaries are clean: no entity belongs to multiple categories. This separation enables independent testing (structural entities can be validated without runtime entities) and independent evolution (adding a new export format doesn't affect structural entities).

variants.architect: Three natural categories emerge that map to architectural layers. Category 1 (Structural: Framework, Series, Round, Question, Choice) forms the schema layer — these entities are immutable, loaded from JSON, and define the system's shape. They follow the Decorator pattern where each level adds context to the level below. Category 2 (Runtime: Session, Answer, Artifact) forms the execution layer — these entities are mutable, persisted to storage, and track user progress. They follow the State pattern where Session's state determines which Questions are available. Category 3 (Output: Export, Project) forms the delivery layer — these entities represent consumable artifacts that the system produces. The classification also follows the Builder pattern: Structural entities are the blueprint, Runtime entities are the construction process, and Output entities are the finished product. The three categories have distinct persistence strategies: Structural entities are serialized as JSON files (immutable), Runtime entities are stored in SQLite (transactional), and Output entities are generated on-demand (ephemeral).
variants.practitioner: The three categories map to src/ subdirectories. Category 1 (Structural) lives in src/data/ — the framework-loader.ts reads JSON files and produces FrameworkDefinition objects. Category 2 (Runtime) lives in src/engine/ and src/storage/ — the engine operates on SessionState, which is persisted by the StorageProvider. Category 3 (Output) lives in src/export/ — the exporters read SessionState and produce ExportResult objects. In practice, the boundaries between categories leak: the ArtifactDictionary (Runtime) is derived from Structural entities (Questions) via src/data/artifact-mapping.ts. The quality scoring in src/intelligence/ reads Runtime entities (Answers) and produces metadata about them. When implementing new features, determine which category the new entity belongs to by asking: (1) Is it loaded from JSON at startup? → Structural. (2) Is it created during a session? → Runtime. (3) Is it generated when the user requests output? → Output.
variants.strategist: The three-category classification maps to three distinct product capabilities: (1) Framework authoring (customizing the 326 probes), (2) Session management (the interactive questioning experience), and (3) Export and delivery (specification output). Each category represents a different user value and monetization opportunity. Category 1 is the intellectual property — the methodology encoded in the 326 probes. A framework marketplace where users can author, share, and sell custom probe sets could be a revenue stream. Category 2 is the user experience — the guided questioning flow, progress tracking, and artifact extraction. This is where UX differentiation matters most. Category 3 is the output — the specification documents that users share with their teams. Export quality directly impacts word-of-mouth adoption. The product strategy should invest disproportionately in Category 2 (experience) because that's where users spend their time, while leveraging Category 1 (content) as the moat and Category 3 (output) as the viral mechanism.
variants.critic: The three-category classification is neat but misses important cross-cutting concerns. The LLM integration layer (src/llm/) doesn't fit cleanly into any category — it operates on Runtime entities (Answers) using Structural entity context (Questions) to produce enhanced Runtime entities (refined Answers, extracted Artifacts). The Intelligence layer (src/intelligence/) similarly spans categories, reading Runtime entities and producing meta-information about them. The event system (SpaceEvent types in types/index.ts) is an orthogonal concern that cuts across all three categories. This categorization also creates a misleading implication that the layers are strictly sequential (define → run → export), when in reality the system supports iterative workflows where users run a session, export a partial spec, refine answers, and re-export. The 'distinct persistence strategies' claim (JSON files for Structural, SQLite for Runtime, on-demand for Output) is incorrect — the framework JSON files are actually compiled into the source code at build time, not loaded dynamically. This means customizing the framework requires rebuilding the tool, which undermines the 'framework authoring' product opportunity.

text: Of the entities listed, which are absolutely essential (core) and which are optional, derivative, or contextual (peripheral)?

choices.text: Most entities are core — the domain has little extraneous surface area
Roughly equal split between core and peripheral entities
A small core (~20%) with a large periphery of optional or derived entities
Core/peripheral depends on use case — context-dependent classification
Entities exist on a spectrum of centrality — no sharp core/peripheral boundary

answer:
Core entities (system cannot function without): Framework, Session, Question, Artifact, Engine. These five entities are the minimal viable set — without any one of them, the system cannot ask questions, record answers, or produce output.

Framework defines what to ask. Question defines individual probes. Session captures the interaction. Artifact extracts structured data. Engine orchestrates the flow.

Peripheral entities (system works but is limited without): Series, Round, Answer, Project, Export.

Series and Round are organizational — they group Questions but the system could theoretically work with a flat list of Questions. Answer is the data record of a Question response — without it, the system would lose history, but the extraction could theoretically happen in real-time. Project is a container — without it, sessions would be unorganized but still functional. Export is a deliverable — without it, the system produces artifacts but no compiled specifications.

The core/peripheral split is important for implementation: core entities get first-class type definitions, comprehensive validation, and priority error handling. Peripheral entities get simpler types and can tolerate graceful degradation (e.g., if Export generation fails, the session data is still preserved).

Context-dependent classification: The Engine becomes peripheral if the system is used as a pure data model (just defining the framework without running it). The Project becomes core if multi-project management is a requirement (which it currently is). This context-dependency is why the entity model includes both perspectives.

variants.architect: The core-peripheral classification follows the concept of essential complexity from Fred Brooks' 'No Silver Bullet.' The 5 core entities (Framework, Session, Question, Artifact, Engine) represent the irreducible complexity of the system — remove any one and the system cannot function. The Engine is the orchestrator that coordinates between Framework (what to ask), Session (what has been answered), and Artifact (what has been extracted). The peripheral entities (Series, Round, Choice, Project, Export) are organizational or additive — they improve usability but the system could theoretically function with a flat list of questions, a simple answer store, and a single export format. The architectural implication is that the core 5 entities should receive the most rigorous type definitions, the most comprehensive test coverage, and the most careful change management. The peripheral entities can be refactored with lower risk.
variants.practitioner: In the codebase, core entities are represented by the most referenced types. FrameworkDefinition is imported by src/data/framework-loader.ts, src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts, and src/engine/question-router.ts. SessionState is imported by src/engine/session-manager.ts, src/engine/core.ts, and all export formatters. QuestionContext is the primary input to the engine's core loop. ArtifactDictionary is consumed by src/data/artifact-mapping.ts, src/llm/artifact-synthesizer.ts, and every exporter. The Engine itself is the main orchestrator in src/engine/core.ts. Peripheral entities have more isolated usage: Series is only accessed through FrameworkDefinition.series, Round is accessed through Series.rounds, Choice is accessed through Question.follow_up_choices, Project is managed by src/storage/, and Export is the output of src/export/. When prioritizing bug fixes or refactoring, core entity issues should be addressed first because their failure cascades to all peripheral consumers.
variants.strategist: The core-peripheral classification has direct product implications. Core entities represent the MVP — without Framework, Session, Question, Artifact, and Engine, there is no product. The minimum viable product ships with these 5 entities and minimal peripheral support (flat question list instead of Series/Round hierarchy, single JSON export instead of 6 formats). The peripheral entities are features that expand the addressable market: the Series/Round hierarchy (Series, Round) enables the 'progressive deepening' UX that appeals to structured thinkers. Multiple export formats (Export) enable integration with existing documentation pipelines. The Project entity enables team collaboration. Product roadmap should invest in core entities first (months 1-3 for CLI MVP), then expand peripheral entities to drive adoption: export formats (months 4-6 for developer adoption), project management (months 7-9 for team adoption), and custom frameworks (months 10-12 for platform play). The core-peripheral distinction also informs pricing: core features are free (OSS CLI), peripheral features are paid (web UI with team features, advanced exports).
variants.critic: The 5-entity core is debatable. The Engine is not an entity — it's a service/controller that operates on entities. Including it in the 'core entity' list conflates the entity model with the service layer, which is an architectural smell. The true core entities are Framework, Session, Question, and Artifact. Engine, Series, Round, and Choice are structural or behavioral concerns, not entities. This misclassification could lead to poor design decisions, like giving Engine persistent state (it shouldn't — it's stateless and operates on SessionState). The claim that 'the system could function with a flat list of questions' understates the importance of the Series/Round structure — without it, the dependency graph cannot function, which means artifacts cannot be consumed by downstream questions. The Series/Round hierarchy is not peripheral; it's essential for the progressive specification methodology that defines SPACE. The peripheral classification of Project is also wrong — multi-session support (Project) is essential for any real-world usage where the first attempt is rarely the final specification.

text: At what level of granularity should entities be modeled? Should fine distinctions be separate entities or attributes of coarser ones?

choices.text: Coarse-grained — entities are broad; most variation is captured via attributes
Moderate — key specializations become distinct entities
Fine-grained — every meaningful distinction yields a separate entity
Mixed — core domains are fine-grained; peripheral domains are coarse
Undecided — granularity should emerge from relationship analysis

answer:
Moderate granularity — key specializations become distinct entities, but trivial variations are collapsed.

Example of appropriate splitting: Session and Answer are separate entities even though Answers live inside Sessions, because Answers have their own lifecycle (they can be edited, skipped, or marked as invalid) and their own relationships (each Answer links to exactly one Question and contributes to specific Artifacts).

Example of appropriate merging: Round and Focus are NOT separate entities. The "focus" is just a string attribute of Round. Splitting them would add complexity without enabling new behaviors.

Example of progressive refinement: The initial model had separate "OpenEndedAnswer" and "MultiChoiceAnswer" entities. These were merged into a single "Answer" entity with a choice_id attribute that may be null (for open-ended only) or populated (for follow-up classification). The split wasn't adding value because both types share the same lifecycle and storage.

Granularity decision criteria: An entity should be separate if it (a) has a distinct lifecycle, (b) participates in unique relationships, (c) has attributes not shared with the candidate parent, or (d) is independently addressable (has its own ID). Question passes all four tests. Round passes tests (a) and (d) but not (b) and (c) — yet it's still separate because it provides essential organizational structure.

The balance: 10 entity types total. Fine enough to capture all meaningful distinctions in the system. Coarse enough to keep the type system manageable. Each entity has 5-15 attributes. The total attribute count across all entities is approximately 80, which is within the cognitive load limit for a single developer.

variants.architect: Moderate granularity is the correct architectural choice because SPACE's entity model serves two masters: the framework definition layer (which benefits from fine-grained entities for flexible question composition) and the session/execution layer (which benefits from coarse-grained entities for simpler state management). The splitting heuristic is: split when two concepts have distinct lifecycles, different relationships to other entities, or when conflating them would violate a business invariant. Following this heuristic: Session and Answer must be separate because a Session persists without Answers (empty session), but an Answer cannot exist without a Session. Question and Choice must be separate because Choices are part of the framework definition (read-only) while Answers to Choices are runtime state. Artifact and Answer must be separate because multiple Answers can produce a single Artifact (synthesized from multiple questions) and one Answer can produce multiple Artifacts.
variants.practitioner: The granularity decision manifests in the TypeScript types. SessionState contains answers as Record<string, AnswerEntry> — answers are embedded in the session, not standalone entities in the storage layer. This means Answer's lifecycle is tied to Session's lifecycle (save session → save answers). FrameworkDefinition contains the question hierarchy as nested arrays (Series → Round → Question → Choice) — this embedding simplifies loading but means individual questions cannot be loaded independently. The ArtifactDictionary is also embedded in SessionState, not a separate entity. The src/storage/sqlite.ts implements separate tables for sessions, answers, and artifacts, but the API layer treats them as a single unit (save/load the entire SessionState). When implementing new features, check whether the new concept needs independent storage (→ make it a separate entity) or can be embedded (→ make it a field or nested type). The practical test: can you query it independently? Artifacts can be queried independently for quality scoring, which is why they have their own storage table.
variants.strategist: The granularity decision impacts feature development velocity. Coarser entities (embedding answers in sessions) mean fewer database tables, simpler queries, and faster implementation. Finer-grained entities (separate answer table with relationships) enable more features (answer history, cross-session comparison, team annotations). The current moderate granularity is appropriate for MVP but will need refinement for the team collaboration feature. Specifically, the Answer entity will need to support: multiple annotations per answer (team members commenting), approval workflows (stakeholder sign-off on answers), and version history (tracking edits). These features require Answer to be a first-class entity with its own lifecycle, not an embedded field in Session. The product decision is when to make this transition — doing it before team features are needed wastes engineering effort, doing it after creates a painful migration. Recommendation: defer the Answer entity extraction until team features are on the roadmap.
variants.critic: The 'moderate granularity' answer is a hedge that avoids committing to a clear position. The reality is that the current implementation has inconsistent granularity: FrameworkDefinition embeds Series/Round/Question/Choice as a deep hierarchy, but SessionState embeds Answers as a flat Record<string, AnswerEntry>. This inconsistency means framework questions can be navigated hierarchically (series → round → question), but answers cannot (you query by question_id, not by series/round/question path). The ArtifactDictionary is a flat Record<string, ArtifactValue> that conflates entity types — 'entity_list' (an array of entity names) and 'domain_scope' (a string description) have completely different value types but share the same dictionary. The 'four-entity-test' described in the existing answer (distinct lifecycle, unique relationships, different attributes, independent query) is too strict — it would keep Question and Choice as the same entity since they share the same lifecycle and can't be queried independently. The granularity problem is that SPACE's model tries to serve both a static definition (framework) and a dynamic execution (session) with overlapping but non-identical entity sets, creating confusion about where boundaries should be drawn.

text: How do entities relate to each other in terms of sharing, inheriting, or differentiating attributes?

choices.text: Mostly independent — entities share few attributes beyond common identifiers
Shared attributes grouped by category — entities in same category share a profile
Inheritance hierarchy — subtypes inherit and extend parent attributes
Mixin / trait composition — entities compose attribute sets from multiple sources
Dynamic — attribute sharing depends on entity state or context

answer:
Shared attributes grouped by functional category:

Universal attributes (shared by most entities): id (unique identifier), created_at (timestamp), updated_at (timestamp). These are present on Session, Answer, Artifact, Project, and Export. Question and Framework use id but not timestamps (they're static definitions).

Structural attributes (shared by definition entities): name, description, text. Framework has name+description. Series has name+description. Round has focus. Question has text. These are all human-readable strings that describe the entity's purpose.

Relational attributes (shared by entities that reference others): The FK pattern appears on Session (project_id → Project), Answer (question_id → Question), Artifact (source_question_id → Question), Export (session_id → Session). The consistency of this pattern (always string FKs, always referencing by ID) simplifies the storage layer.

Content attributes (unique to each entity): Framework has depends_on/provides/consumes arrays. Session has answers/artifacts dictionaries. Answer has open_ended/choice_id. Artifact has key/value/confidence. These are the distinguishing attributes that make each entity type necessary.

The dependency graph between Series creates a cross-cutting concern: Series entities have both structural attributes (name, description, rounds) and dependency attributes (deps, consumes, provides). The consumes/provides arrays use string keys that must match artifact dictionary keys — this implicit contract is enforced at runtime by the question router, not at compile time. A type-safe artifact key type could improve this.

variants.architect: Entity relationships follow three patterns: composition (Framework owns Series, Series owns Round), reference (Answer references Question, Artifact references Question), and aggregation (Project contains Sessions). The shared attributes (id, created_at, updated_at) are universal value object fields that could be extracted into a base type. The differentiation follows the Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) model for ArtifactValue, where the value attribute can hold any type and the key provides semantic meaning. Inheritance is minimal — there's no type hierarchy among entities, which is a deliberate design choice to keep the model flat and simple. The relationship between Framework entities (definition) and Session entities (runtime) is the most architecturally significant: they share the same keys (question IDs, series numbers) but have different lifecycles and storage strategies. This is the Foreign Key pattern where Answer.question_id references Question.id across the definition/runtime boundary.
variants.practitioner: Shared attributes are implemented as base interfaces that concrete entities extend. The id field is typed as string (UUID for runtime entities, hierarchical string like '1.1.1' for definition entities). The created_at/updated_at fields use ISO 8601 strings (not Date objects) for serialization compatibility — this is enforced in src/types/index.ts. The relationship between Answer and Question is maintained by the question_id field in AnswerEntry, which must match a valid question ID in the framework definition. The src/engine/validator.ts checks this referential integrity when answers are submitted. The ArtifactValue.source_question_id provides the reverse reference — tracing artifacts back to their source questions. The src/data/artifact-mapping.ts defines the mapping between question IDs and artifact keys, which is the schema for the reference relationship. When implementing cross-referencing features, use the question ID as the canonical join key between definition and runtime entities.
variants.strategist: The entity relationships reveal the product's data model for team features. The Project → Session → Answer hierarchy enables a 'project workspace' where multiple team members complete sessions independently, and their answers are compared and merged. The Answer → Question reference enables 'question assignment' where different team members answer different questions (the architect answers Series 3 questions, the PM answers Series 1 questions). The Artifact → Question provenance (source_question_id) enables 'answer traceability' where stakeholders can see which answers contributed to which specification sections. These team features justify the transition from free CLI to paid web platform. The relationship model also supports 'framework customization' where users modify the question set — the composition relationship (Framework → Series → Round → Question) would need to become a reference relationship to support user-authored questions. This is a major architectural change that should be planned for the platform roadmap.
variants.critic: The entity relationship model has a significant flaw: it assumes a single framework version per project, but the relationship between Session.framework_version and FrameworkDefinition is implicit (matched by string comparison) rather than explicit (foreign key with constraint). If a framework is updated and a session was created with the old version, there's no mechanism to detect or handle the mismatch. The ArtifactValue derived_from field (string[]) claims to track multi-hop derivation chains, but the artifact extraction in src/data/artifact-mapping.ts doesn't populate this field — it's aspirational, not implemented. The shared attributes (id, created_at, updated_at) are defined inconsistently: SessionMeta has them, but ArtifactValue does not (it has source_question_id and last_updated but no id or created_at). This inconsistency means artifacts cannot be individually tracked, versioned, or deleted. The EAV pattern for ArtifactDictionary is a known anti-pattern that sacrifices query performance and type safety for flexibility — a typed artifact registry would be more maintainable.

text: What are the systemic boundaries of this domain? What is explicitly in scope vs. out of scope?

choices.text: Tightly bounded — scope is narrow and well-defined
Moderately bounded — clear core with some fuzzy edges
Loosely bounded — domain bleeds into adjacent areas
Bounded by role/perspective — different stakeholders draw different boundaries
Boundaries are discovered — scoping is itself a goal of the process

answer:
